big_idea: A Pattern Conductor doesn't just predict — they JUSTIFY using the rule, the start, and the number of jumps.
learning_intention: We are learning to predict terms far beyond what is shown in a pattern and to justify our predictions formally using the rule, the starting value, and the number of jumps.
student_learning_goal: I can predict term 50 of a pattern and justify my prediction using the rule and the term number.
success_criteria: I can predict term 30, term 50, or term 100 of a growing pattern using the rule rather than drawing every term.
I can produce a full justification sentence: 'I started at ___, the rule is ___, I jumped ___ times, so term ___ is ___.'
I can spot when my partner's prediction is wrong and explain WHY using the rule.
lesson_specific_materials: Anchor chart from previous lessons (PATTERN, OPERATION, +N RULE, ×N RULE, COMPOUND RULE, TABLE OF VALUES up — add JUSTIFY and GENERALIZE today)

Three pre-built broken patterns / far-prediction setups: (1) growing +7 starting at 7 with terms 1-3 visible (7, 14, 21) and gap at term 5, (2) shrinking -8 starting at 80 with terms 1-3 visible (80, 72, 64) and gap at term 7, (3) compound +5 then -1 starting at 10 with terms 1-4 visible (10, 15, 14, 19) and far-prediction prompt for term 20
Number line 0-1000 visible on the math wall, plus thousand chart for reference
JUSTIFY and GENERALIZE hand-printed on chart paper
Justification sentence frame card (one large class version, smaller versions for each pair): 'I started at ___, the rule is ___, I jumped ___ times, so term ___ is ___.'
Class formative tracker for Lesson 4 (provided in assessment_suite stage)
Calculators (one per pair) — Grade 3 children may use calculators for the multiplicative arithmetic in this lesson

minds_on.hook: Coco wrote three patterns on the board with HUGE gaps — term 5, term 7, term 20. We don't have time to draw every cell. Today we use the rule to JUMP.
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Lay the three setup patterns in a line. Hold up Coco.

Say to students: 'Pattern Conductors, Coco needs help. Three patterns. Each one needs us to find a faraway term — but we cannot draw every cell. We have to JUMP using the rule. Then we have to JUSTIFY — explain WHY our answer is right. That's the Grade 3 move.'

Point to setup 1 (7, 14, 21, ?, term 5). 'Read the visible terms.' (7, 14, 21.) 'Rule?' (+7, or term × 7.) 'Term 4?' (28.) 'Term 5?' Take responses. (35.) 'How did you know? JUSTIFY.' Listen for: 'Term 5 = 5 × 7 = 35' OR 'I added 7 to term 4 (28).' Validate both. Tape JUSTIFY to the chart.

Point to setup 2 (80, 72, 64, ?, term 7). 'Read.' (80, 72, 64.) 'Rule?' (-8.) 'Term 7?' Take a moment. 'I started at 80, the rule is -8, I jumped 6 times, so term 7 is 80 - (6 × 8) = 80 - 48 = 32.' Have the class chant the sentence frame. 'I started at ___, the rule is ___, I jumped ___ times, so term ___ is ___.' Tape GENERALIZE to the chart.

Point to setup 3 (10, 15, 14, 19, term 20). 'This one is COMPOUND. Rule: +5 then -1. Net effect of one cycle (+5 -1) = +4 every 2 terms. From term 1 to term 20 is 19 jumps, which is 9 full cycles of 2 (18 jumps, ending at term 19, value 10 + 9 × 4 = 46) plus one more jump (+5 because odd-position jumps are +5) → term 20 = 51.' This is hard. We will work through it together in partners.
student_actions: Sit in a circle on the carpet, facing the three pre-built setups.
Read the visible terms of each pattern aloud and identify the rule.
Predict the requested far term and try to justify aloud using the sentence frame.
Repeat the words 'justify' and 'generalize' aloud as a class.
Watch the teacher chant the justification frame: 'I started at ___, the rule is ___, I jumped ___ times, so term ___ is ___.'

action.activity_name: Detectives at Work — Predict Far, Justify Always

steps.instruction: Whole-class far-prediction model: take a fresh growing pattern (rule +6 starting at 6). Compute term 10 together via the multiplication shortcut: 10 × 6 = 60. Then chant the justification: 'I started at 6, the rule is +6, I jumped 9 times to reach term 10, so term 10 = 6 + 9 × 6 = 6 + 54 = 60.' Also accept: 'Term 10 = 10 × 6 = 60.' Write both versions on the board.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Two ways to justify the same answer. The first uses the starting value plus jumps. The second uses term × rule. Both are correct. The deeper move is — your justification has to mention the RULE, not just the answer.'

steps.instruction: Partner round 1 — single-step far prediction. Pairs predict term 30 of an assigned +N or -N rule and justify using the sentence frame. Calculators allowed. Each pair gets Animal Cards (M1), Parade Strip (M2), Core Loop Frame (M5), and a justification frame card. Both partners must say the sentence aloud at least once.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'You and your partner just got a +N or -N rule. Compute term 30. Use the sentence frame to justify. Both partners must say the sentence aloud at least once. Then switch.'

steps.instruction: Partner round 2 — multiplicative far prediction. Pairs swap and now work on a ×2 or ×3 rule with a small starting value. Predict term 5, term 7, term 10. By term 10 some values will exceed 1000 — pairs should notice the ceiling and discuss when their pattern crosses it.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Multiplicative rule. Smaller starting number this time. Predict terms 5, 7, AND 10. Use a calculator. When a value exceeds 1000, write OFF THE CHART and tell me about it during share circle.'

steps.instruction: Partner round 3 — backward justification: pairs build a pattern with one VISIBLE term in the middle (e.g., term 5 = 32) and a known rule (×2). They reason BACKWARD to find term 1. Justify using the sentence frame: 'Term 5 = 32, the rule is ×2, I jumped backward 4 times by dividing by 2 four times, so term 1 = 32 ÷ 16 = 2.'
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Backward justification. Given term 5 and the rule, find term 1. The justification frame is the same — but you say "jumped BACKWARD" instead of forward. Try it.'

steps.instruction: Stretch challenge — compound rule far prediction. Pairs build a multi-step compound rule (e.g., +5 then -2 starting at 10) and predict term 30 by reasoning about the cycle net-effect. Use the full sentence frame and include the words 'per cycle of 2' in the justification.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to extending pairs: 'Compound rule, term 30. Use the cycle net-effect reasoning we discussed in Lesson 2. Justify using the full frame, including the words "per cycle".'

steps.instruction: Whole-class debrief AND circulate-track: bring 2-3 pairs back to share justifications aloud. Add new GENERALIZATIONS to the anchor chart (e.g., 'For a +N rule starting at N, term K = K × N'). While pairs continue working, use the Lesson 4 formative tracker — look for: multiplication shortcut versus drawing, full justification sentence with rule language, backward reasoning, 1000 ceiling awareness for multiplicative rules.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Two pairs share a justification — we will write the GENERAL RULE you discovered on the chart.' Then walk between remaining pairs. Pick one child per pair. Ask: 'What is term 30?' Then: 'JUSTIFY using the sentence frame.' Then: 'How did you know it was multiplication, not addition?' Record on the tracker.

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay with single-step +N rules and small N (+2, +3, +5) starting at small numbers. Predict only term 10 (not term 30). Provide the sentence frame pre-printed and encourage the child to fill the blanks orally before writing. Pair with a confident peer. Use a calculator for any multiplication.
differentiation.for_extending: Use multiplicative rules (×2, ×3, ×5) and multi-step compound rules. Predict term 50 AND term 100. Stretch question: 'For your rule, what is the LATEST term that stays under 1000?' (Requires solving an inequality — let them estimate by trial-and-error multiplication.)
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Use a sentence frame: 'Start = ___. Rule = ___. Jumps = ___. Term ___ = ___.' Pre-fill the start and rule for the child. Allow gestures and pointing as part of the justification. Provide a calculator from the start. Use a partner who can scribe.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: After predicting, the pair PHYSICALIZES the jumps. Each step forward is one jump. They walk from term 1 to term 30 (30 small steps), counting aloud. Then for the multiplicative rule, they DOUBLE their step size each jump (1 step, then 2 steps, then 4 steps...) until they can't take any more steps in the room — which physically demonstrates the 1000 ceiling.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Can the child predict term 30, 50, or 100 using the rule rather than drawing? Do they use the multiplication shortcut for additive rules (term × N for +N starting at N)? Do they produce the full justification sentence with rule language? Can they reason backward to find an earlier term given a later one? Do they articulate the 1000 ceiling for fast-growing multiplicative rules?
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the appropriate column on the Lesson 4 formative tracker.
tracker_columns: Reasons backward to find earlier term

discussion_prompts: Who computed the BIGGEST term value today? What was the rule, the term, and the value?
When did you use multiplication as a SHORTCUT instead of skip-counting? Why was multiplication faster?
If your rule is ×3 starting at 3, at what term does the value cross 1000?
Coco wants to know — what is the difference between PREDICTING and JUSTIFYING? Can you predict without justifying? Can you justify without predicting?
What is one GENERALIZATION you discovered today that we can write on the class chart?
consolidation.exit_routine: On the way out the door, each child says one full justification sentence using the frame: 'I started at ___, the rule is ___, I jumped ___ times, so term ___ is ___.' Teacher records who can produce the frame fluently versus who needs more practice.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Class formative tracker for C1.3 (justification + far prediction) plus completed student worksheet 'Justify the Faraway Term'.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Far prediction with formal justification is the deepest C1.3 marker for Grade 3 — it separates children who pattern-match from children who reason about the rule as a generalizable shortcut and ARTICULATE that reasoning. The teacher needs evidence of who can do this independently before the Lesson 5 summative requires it. Children who predict correctly but cannot justify are often almost-there — they need the sentence-frame scaffold for one more session before the summative.

expanded_walkthrough.title: Far-Term Prediction with Justification — the G3 marker
expanded_walkthrough.rationale: L4 introduces the G3 capstone reasoning: predicting term 30, 50, even 100 using only the rule, AND writing a JUSTIFICATION sentence using a structured frame. The double demand (compute + justify) is what the EQAO Algebra block tests. Step 2 (single-step far prediction with sentence frame) and Step 3 (multiplicative far prediction) are the keystones. Step 4 (backward justification) is the stretch — most G3 children can predict forward but struggle to reason backward from a known term.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Carpet has the +6 demo with the multiplication shortcut written out (term 10 = 10 × 6 = 60). Anchor chart has the JUSTIFICATION SENTENCE FRAME visible: 'Term ___ is ___ because the rule is ___ and we did ___ jumps from term 1.' Each pair has white-boards, Animal Cards, Parade Strip, calculators, and a copy of the sentence frame card. Teacher's clipboard has the new G3 columns: 'predicts without drawing', 'justifies with the frame', 'reasons backward'.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Whole-class demo: lay out a +6 rule starting at 6. Term 1 = 6, term 2 = 12, term 3 = 18. 'Term 10?' Children may start drawing — STOP them. 'Use the rule. Term 10 is term 1 plus NINE jumps of +6. That's 6 plus 9 times 6. Or, 10 times 6 is 60.' Walk through the multiplication: 'For a +N rule starting at N, term K is K times N.' Mark this on the anchor chart as a GENERALIZATION. Now: 'Term 30?' Same shortcut: 30 × 6 = 180. 'Term 100?' 100 × 6 = 600. The shortcut scales.

Walk to a pair predicting term 30 of their assigned +N rule. They'll often skip-count by hand all 30 terms. Stop them. 'Don't draw. Use the rule. Term 30 is term 1 plus 29 jumps of +N.' Now make them write the justification sentence using the frame: 'Term 30 is ___ because the rule is +N and we did 29 jumps from term 1.' Listen for the '29 jumps' specifically — most children write '30 jumps' first time because they miscount the gap from term 1 to term 30. The off-by-one is the diagnostic.

For the multiplicative round: a pair has ×2 starting at 1. Term 5? 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 — they can compute. Term 7? 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. Term 10? They'll try to compute 1024 by hand and get lost. 'Calculator allowed. Use the rule.' For ×2 starting at 1, term K is 2 to the (K-1). Most G3 children won't have exponent notation yet — that's OK, they should still be able to chain it on the calculator.

For backward justification (Step 4): pair has term 5 = 32 with a ×2 rule. They must find term 1. Walk: 'If we DOUBLE going forward, what do we do going BACKWARD?' Some will say 'halve'. 'Yes. Term 5 is 32. Term 4 is 32 ÷ 2 = 16. Term 3 = 8. Term 2 = 4. Term 1 = 2.' Many children stall here. The two-axis thinking — operation has an INVERSE — is genuinely new for G3.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Draws every intermediate term; cannot use the rule as a shortcut.
(Mid) Predicts term 10 using skip-counting on fingers but stalls at term 30+. Justification sentence has off-by-one error.
(Strong) Uses K × N shortcut for +N rules. Writes a complete justification with correct jump count.
(Stretched) Articulates the general formula (term K is start plus (K-1) × N) AND can reason backward via the inverse operation.
common_misconceptions: Term K means K jumps from term 1. (Off-by-one — it's K-1 jumps.)
Far prediction means draw faster. (Child still draws every term, just abbreviates.)
Multiplicative rules don't have shortcuts. (Child thinks only +N has the K × N pattern.)
Backward inference is a different skill from forward inference. (Child can predict term 30 forward but cannot find term 1 from term 5.)
recovery_moves: Pencil-down audit. After every prediction, ask: 'Did you USE the rule, or DRAW the parade?' The verbal commitment to the shortcut reinforces it.
Sentence frame discipline. Don't accept a number; require the full sentence. The 'jumps from term 1' phrasing self-corrects the off-by-one.
Inverse-operation chant: 'plus and minus are inverses; times and divide are inverses'. Make the pairing explicit at the chart level.
Backward worked-example. Solve term 5 → term 1 together. Make the inversion physically visible by sliding cards leftward.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of C1.3 — predicting terms far beyond what is shown using the rule, AND producing formal justifications using the sentence frame.

parts_outline.task: Show three patterns with the first 4 terms visible. Pattern A: 9, 18, 27, 36 (rule +9). Pattern B: 100, 92, 84, 76 (rule -8). Pattern C: 2, 6, 18, 54 (rule ×3). For each: 'Rule: ____. Term 10: ____. Justify: I started at ___, the rule is ___, I jumped ___ times, so term 10 is ___.'
Show a partial table of values with TERM 1, 2, 3, 4, 30 and VALUE 25, 50, 75, 100, ___. Student fills in term 30 AND writes a full justification sentence below the table using the frame.
Detective scenario with backward reasoning: 'Coco's pattern has rule ×2. Term 7 = 64. Find term 1 AND term 10.' Student fills both, then writes a full justification for each.
